frontMatter.title: How is Australia’s population distributed, and what might explain one pattern?
frontMatter.description: A 60-minute population inquiry. Sources A and B measure population, not the distribution of jobs, services or infrastructure. Those are possible explanations to test with further evidence. Follow the website and write in your exercise book: learn (10 min), understand (10), investigate (15), explain (15), reflect (10). Complete your attempt before teacher-led feedback; models remain in the separate teacher guide.

frontMatter.title: What successful geographical reasoning looks like
frontMatter.description: Record the lesson title and date in your exercise book. By the end you should be able to:
intentions: Distinguish urbanisation (a rising urban share) from urban population growth.
Describe located distribution patterns and settlement arrangements using evidence.
Interpret population counts, annual growth rates and modelled density without mixing them.
Explain possible influences, distinguish inference from observation and identify evidence needed to test a claim.

completion.description: Ask your teacher to review your completed exercise-book responses using the separate model answers and criteria. Improve one explanation using the criteria; tell your teacher what still needs clarification. Reaching this page does not certify mastery.

activities.title: Urbanisation: share or number? · 4 min
activities.lede: Read the explanation, then record the three essential notes in your exercise book.

notes.body: Urban population growth means an increase in the number of urban residents. Urbanisation means an increase in their share of the total population. The two measures answer different questions.
If urban and rural populations grow at the same rate, urban numbers rise but the urban share stays the same. Definitions of urban areas also differ between countries, so comparisons need care.

image.alt: Illustrative comparison: the urban share rises from 40 per cent to 50 per cent; the rural share falls from 60 per cent to 50 per cent. Each bar represents the entire population at that time.
image.caption: Illustrative proportions, not measured places or years. Each bar represents 100% of the population.
image.source: Concepts: UN DESA, World Urbanization Prospects 2025 glossary
image.rights: Original OnlineLessonMaker explanatory diagram, reused unchanged from the approved G03 fixture. No UN artwork reproduced.

keyNotes: Urbanisation means a rising urban share of the population.
Urban population growth means more urban residents, even if their share stays unchanged.
Check the definition of “urban” before comparing places.

activities.title: Test the difference · 4 min

notes.body: Imagine a population with 40 urban and 60 rural residents. If both groups grow by 20%, there are 48 urban and 72 rural residents. The urban population has grown, but its share is still 40%. These figures are illustrative, not observations from a real place.

keyNotes: A population count is a number of people.
A population proportion compares a group with the whole.
activities.lede: This imagined place is not evidence about Australia. Work in your exercise book before moving on.

questions.stem: In the illustrative place, 40 urban and 60 rural residents each increase by 20%.
parts: Calculate each new count and the new total.
Calculate the new urban share. Is this urban population growth, urbanisation, both or neither? Explain.
questions.answer: 48 urban; 72 rural; 120 total; urban share 40%. Urban population growth without urbanisation.
questions.workedAnswer: Forty multiplied by 1.2 is 48; sixty multiplied by 1.2 is 72. Divide 48 by 120 and multiply by 100: 40%. More urban residents does not by itself show a rising urban share.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. Accept equivalent evidence-based wording.

activities.title: Where people live · 5 min
activities.lede: Record the notes; use the diagram to describe arrangement, not causes.

notes.body: Population distribution is the pattern of where people live. Density is population divided by area, measured here in people per km². A large population and a high density are different things.

Settlements can be clustered, linear (along a route or valley), or dispersed. A settlement hierarchy describes differences in size and function: a small settlement may serve local needs, while a larger centre may provide more specialised services. These are useful descriptions, not a ranking of the value of communities.
Describe location, concentration, gaps and exceptions. A population map shows where people are estimated to live; it does not directly show their reasons for living there.

keyNotes: Distribution describes where; density is people per unit of area.
Describe a located pattern and an exception before proposing a cause.
Settlement size, arrangement and function are related but different.

image.alt: Three explicitly illustrative settlement arrangements: buildings grouped closely in a cluster, arranged in a line, and spread apart. No real place or scale is represented.
image.caption: Original schematic: symbols represent settlements or buildings at an unspecified scale. This is a vocabulary aid, not measured geographical evidence.
image.rights: Original lesson artwork; no copied geographical geometry.

examples.label: Read, compare, qualify · 5 min
examples.prompt: Read Source B, then follow the complete worked comparison. Why can the largest increase and the fastest growth describe different places?

steps.text: Identify: Source B is the ABS 27 March 2025 release. Its June 2024 ERP is preliminary in this dated release and may be revised later. It compares ERP for four selected GCCSAs, with changes over 2023–24. These are broad city regions, not four equally sized built-up areas.
Read: Melbourne added 142,637 residents, compared with Perth’s 72,742. Melbourne therefore had the larger numerical increase of this pair.

Calculate and compare: Melbourne’s earlier population was 5,350,705 − 142,637 = 5,208,068; 142,637 ÷ 5,208,068 × 100 ≈ 2.7%. Perth’s was 2,384,371 − 72,742 = 2,311,629; 72,742 ÷ 2,311,629 × 100 ≈ 3.1%. Perth grew faster proportionally because the change is measured against a smaller starting population.

Conclude with a limit: more added residents and a faster percentage growth are different measures. These selected city-region changes do not establish Australia’s urbanisation: a consistent urban definition and national urban/total populations over time would also be needed.

activities.title: Investigate Source A · 8 min
activities.practiceNote: Write in your exercise book. Read the four questions for this map first, then choose Inspect source. Select Fit source, then Zoom in (+) to read the legend and regional pattern; use the arrow keys to pan and 0 to fit again. Task shows the map-reading reminder; Source details gives provenance. Close returns to these questions. Record observations before explanations.

questions.stem: Use Source A in Inspect source, then answer in your exercise book.
parts: Identify the producer, population reference date, unit and what each coloured grid cell represents.
Describe two located concentrations and contrast them with a broad interior area. Name regions, not exact streets.
Identify an exception to “everyone lives on the east coast”. Use the map, not a guess.
Explain why a grey cell and a national-scale thumbnail do not prove that a place has no people, communities, activity or significance.
questions.answer: ABS, June 2024; modelled people per 1 km². Concentrations along eastern/south-eastern Australia and a separate south-western concentration contrast with much of the interior. The south-west is an exception to the east-coast-only claim. Modelled zero is not proof of absence.
questions.workedAnswer: A strong description locates the eastern/south-eastern concentrations and contrasts them with extensive grey interior cells. The south-western concentration is an explicit exception. Smaller inland and northern patches also prevent a coast-only absolute claim. The grid models resident population from SA1 estimates and residential address points; modelling, reduction and the time reference limit fine-scale conclusions. Do not interpret grey as unoccupied Country or absence of Aboriginal communities.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. Credit located observations, a map-supported exception, correct density units and an explicit model/scale limitation.

activities.title: Investigate Source B · 7 min
activities.practiceNote: Answer in your exercise book. Include units and the period. Keep a count, a percentage growth rate and a density separate.

questions.stem: Compare Sydney and Brisbane using Source B.
parts: Which had more residents in June 2024? By how many?
Which added more residents in 2023–24? By how many? Which had the higher percentage growth?
Why can you not use these four rows to state Australia’s urban share or rank these regions by density?
questions.answer: Sydney had 2,777,170 more residents and added 34,608 more residents than Brisbane. Brisbane’s growth rate was higher: 2.7% compared with 2.0%. Urban share and density cannot be obtained from these rows alone.
questions.workedAnswer: Subtract 2,780,063 from 5,557,233 to obtain 2,777,170 residents. Subtract 72,930 from 107,538 to obtain 34,608 added residents. Compare the published rates separately. The table lacks the whole national urban population and total population under a consistent urban classification; it also lacks land areas. GCCSAs include non-urban land and are not a national urban/rural classification.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. Accept equivalent evidence-based wording.

activities.title: From pattern to possible explanation · 4 min
activities.lede: Sources A and B show population evidence, not where economic activities occur. Jobs, services and infrastructure are possible influences requiring separate evidence.

notes.body: Access to jobs, transport and services can attract people and activities to centres. Water availability and terrain can affect settlement opportunities. Existing investment and past decisions can reinforce concentrations. These are general mechanisms to investigate, not causes proved by Source A.

A density map does not show employment, rainfall, land-use decisions, migration motives or cultural connections. Low modelled density must not be described as worthless land or empty Country. Communities and connections to Country cannot be read off a population colour.

Link an observation to a possible mechanism, then name additional evidence at an appropriate date and scale. For example, transport and employment evidence could test a jobs-and-access explanation; rainfall and water-supply evidence could test a water explanation.

keyNotes: Separate what Source A shows from the causes you infer.
Use “may” or “could” when the supplied evidence does not establish a cause.
Name additional evidence that would test your proposed explanation.

activities.title: Plan an explanation · 3 min
activities.practiceNote: Plan four short points in your exercise book, using Sources A and B below. This is a plan, not a second full paragraph. Your teacher holds the model answer until after your attempt.

questions.stem: Explain a concentration shown on Source A.
parts: Observation: locate one concentration and contrast it with another region.
Evidence: identify the source date, what the colour represents and a relevant numerical comparison from B. Do not treat city counts as density.
Inference: propose one possible influence and explain the mechanism.
Qualification: name a missing source that could test the inference and explain one limit of A or B.
questions.answer: A complete response combines a located map observation, accurately labelled evidence, a possible mechanism and a test/limitation.
questions.workedAnswer: Source A’s June 2024 grid shows concentrated populated cells along eastern and south-eastern Australia compared with much of the interior. Source B separately records 5,557,233 residents in Greater Sydney and 2,780,063 in Greater Brisbane; those are city-region counts, not density values. Access to employment and services may help concentrate settlement because people can seek work and services near established centres. A dated employment-and-transport map would help test that mechanism; neither A nor B directly measures motives or proves the cause.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. Accept equivalent evidence-based wording.

activities.title: Explain one population pattern · 8 min
activities.practiceNote: Core: write 60–90 words (about four or five sentences) in your exercise book. Use 2 min to select evidence and plan, 5 min to write, and 1 min to check. Sources A and B are below. Extension, if ready: add a second possible mechanism and develop the response towards 100–140 words. Complete your attempt before teacher-led feedback.

questions.stem: How is Australia’s population distributed, and what might explain one pattern? Use Sources A and B.
parts: Describe a located distribution pattern from A and one exception.
Support your response with one accurate comparison from B, stating date/period and units.
Explain one possible influence and how it might affect the pattern. Employment, services and infrastructure are hypotheses here, not activities directly measured by A or B.
State a source limitation and propose specific additional evidence to test one explanation.
questions.answer: Core criteria: a located pattern and exception; an accurate labelled comparison; one qualified mechanism; a specific source limitation and proposed test. Extension: develop a second mechanism. The original longer model remains an extension example in the teacher guide.
questions.workedAnswer: Australia’s June 2024 modelled grid shows concentrations along eastern and south-eastern Australia compared with much of the interior; the south-western concentration is an exception to an east-coast-only description. In the ABS 2023–24 release, Greater Sydney had 5,557,233 residents and Greater Brisbane 2,780,063 at June 2024: these are city-region counts, not densities. Employment and service access may attract residents towards established centres. Earlier infrastructure investment may reinforce that clustering by improving access. These mechanisms are inferences: the map does not record people’s reasons for settling. Comparing dated employment and transport evidence with the grid could test the access explanation. Modelled 1 km² cells and national-scale reduction also limit conclusions about individual homes or communities.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. See teacher guide analytic rubric. Accept different mechanisms when explained and appropriately qualified; do not require this sample paragraph. Core is 60–90 words, one mechanism, within 8 minutes. The preserved 113-word workedAnswer is an extension model, not the minimum expected response.

activities.title: Check, revise and reflect · 10 min
activities.practiceNote: Write short answers in your exercise book (5 min), then improve your inquiry paragraph (3 min). Use the final 2 min to record one remaining question. After completing your attempt, move to Completion and compare with the criteria during teacher-led feedback. Completion alone does not demonstrate mastery.

questions.stem: Correct the claims and revise your explanation.
parts: “More city residents always means urbanisation.” Use the illustrative 40/60 example to correct this.
“A red density cell means the fastest population growth.” Identify the missing evidence.
“The map proves everyone moves to the coast for jobs.” Separate the overstatement, observation and untested cause.
Revise one sentence in your independent response to make its evidence or uncertainty more precise. Record one question that A and B cannot answer.
questions.answer: Urban growth can occur at an unchanged urban share; density is not change; neither a universal coast-only pattern nor a migration motive is proved. Revision should improve source use or qualification.
questions.workedAnswer: The illustrative population grows from 40 urban of 100 to 48 of 120: still 40% urban, so growth without urbanisation. A red cell is a high modelled density for June 2024; comparable populations at two dates would be needed for growth. A shows concentrations plus exceptions, not everyone’s movement or motives. A useful revision names a source/date/unit, replaces “proves” with a qualified inference, or adds the evidence needed to test it.
questions.teacherNote: Y9-01 TEACHER ONLY: assess geographical reasoning, not a single memorised paragraph. Accept equivalent evidence-based wording.
